The old lighthouse had not guided a ship in forty years, yet its keeper still climbed the spiral stairs every dusk. His name was Elias, and the townspeople below thought him a relic, a man polishing a dead star. But Elias knew something they had forgotten: light is not only for ships.

Each evening, he cleaned the great lens with a soft cloth, whispering apologies to its dusty prisms. When the lamp flickered alive, the beam swept across the black water like a slow, patient arm reaching for someone lost. Gulls circled the gallery, and the wind tapped the glass as if asking to come in.

One night, a girl from the village followed him up the stairs. She was angry at the world, she said, and wanted to see whether anything still mattered. Elias handed her the lantern key. She turned it, and the lighthouse blazed.

Out on the dark sea, a small fishing boat changed course, just slightly, away from the rocks. The girl stared.

“It still matters,” Elias said.

She visited every week after that. She learned the lens, the tides, the language of storms. When Elias grew too old to climb, she climbed for him.

And the lighthouse, though the ships had mostly gone, kept burning, not because it was needed by everyone, but because it was needed by someone. Somewhere, a traveler saw it and remembered that hope often shines brightest when it seems useless. Even small lights can keep the dark from winning, forever.
